notes: Source claim: a process is a running program, and the OS creates the illusion of many CPUs by time sharing one or a few physical CPUs; the stated cost is slower per-process progress while the CPU is shared.
Source claim: a process's machine state is an inventory of its address space, registers (including the program counter and stack pointer), and I/O state such as open files.
Source claim: any process API needs create, destroy, wait, miscellaneous control (suspend/resume), and status operations; the chapter presents these as generic rather than UNIX-specific.

Source claim: creation loads code and static data, allocates and initializes the stack with argc/argv, may allocate a heap, sets up standard file descriptors, and then jumps to main(); loading may be eager or lazy.

Source claim: the simplified states are running, ready, and blocked, with scheduled/descheduled and I/O initiate/complete transitions; xv6 adds unused, embryonic, sleeping, runnable, and zombie states.

Source claim: xv6's struct proc stores memory bounds, kernel stack, state, pid, parent, sleep channel, open files, cwd, saved register context, and trap frame; a context switch saves and restores that register context.
Source claim: a zombie has exited but not been reaped; the parent's wait() retrieves the exit status and releases the remaining process structures.

notes: [Source] The chapter frames CPU virtualization as a two-constraint problem: direct execution buys performance, while limits buy control, and it states that both hardware and OS support are required (sections 6.1-6.2).

[Source] Two execution modes are the primitive: user mode blocks privileged operations such as I/O and trap-table installation, kernel mode permits them, and the trap instruction is the only sanctioned crossing (section 6.2, tip on protected control transfer).

[Source] Trap dispatch is indirected through a boot-time trap table and a system-call number rather than a user-supplied jump address; the chapter explicitly calls this indirection a form of protection (section 6.2).
[Source] Figure 6.2 decomposes the protocol into boot-time setup (trap table, first timer arming) and per-run transitions, with hardware saving registers onto a per-process kernel stack.

[Source] Cooperative relinquishment through system calls, yield, or faults cannot bound a spinning process; the timer interrupt is presented as the minimal hardware addition that restores OS control without process cooperation (section 6.3).

[Source] The context switch is described as two separate save/restore pairs: implicit hardware saves on trap, then explicit software saves into the process structure inside switch(); changing the kernel stack pointer is what makes return-from-trap resume B instead of A (section 6.3, Figure 6.3).

[Source] The xv6 swtch listing in Figure 6.4 makes the mechanism concrete: the return address is popped into the old context, %esp is stored, then a fresh return address is pushed and ret resumes the new context.

[Source] Section 6.4 concedes that an interrupt during trap handling is a real problem and defers it to the concurrency material, sketching interrupt disabling while flagging lost interrupts as the cost of overusing it.

[Inference] The lmbench figures quoted in the context-switch aside are 1996 hardware measurements plus a qualitative modern remark, so they are not usable as a current latency budget without fresh measurement.

[Inference] The baby-proofing analogy implies a perimeter security posture: once traps and the timer are configured, the kernel still has to distrust the arguments crossing the boundary, which is the residual attack surface the user-input tip names.

notes: [Source] Policy is built by progressively relaxing five stated workload assumptions; the chapter singles out known job runtime as the worst offender because it would make the scheduler omniscient (section 7.1).
[Source] Turnaround time is completion minus arrival, which collapses to completion time under simultaneous arrivals; FIFO averages 110 seconds on the 100/10/10 example (sections 7.2-7.3).
[Source] The convoy effect names FIFO's failure when a long job blocks short ones, and SJF lowers that same example's average turnaround to 50 seconds (sections 7.3-7.4).
[Source] SJF is non-preemptive, so short jobs arriving late still wait; STCF preempts and re-ranks by remaining time on each arrival, reaching 50 seconds in the late-arrival example (section 7.5).

[Source] Response time is first-run minus arrival, the metric under which STCF is poor and round robin strong: 1 second average versus 5 seconds in the three-job, five-second example (sections 7.6-7.7).

[Source] Time-slice length is an explicit trade-off: shorter slices improve response time while context-switch cost, including cache, TLB and branch-predictor state, must be amortized, so the slice cannot shrink without bound (section 7.7, tip on amortization).

[Source] Round robin is called nearly pessimal for turnaround (average 14 seconds in the same example), and the chapter generalizes that any policy fair on a small time scale will trade away turnaround time (section 7.7).

[Source] I/O is folded in by treating each CPU burst as an independent job, so a blocked process yields the CPU and its next burst can preempt a long CPU-bound job, producing overlap and better utilization (section 7.8).

[Inference] The claim that STCF is provably optimal is scoped to the chapter's assumptions and the single turnaround metric; it is not evidence for multicore, multi-metric, or I/O-heavy behavior, which the text does not analyze.

[Inference] The assumption ladder is a reusable audit device: a workload profile could record which assumptions (equal length, known runtime, no I/O, run to completion) are violated and which single metric the design is optimizing.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Distinguish response time from turnaround time explicitly: the chapter shows a policy can be excellent on first-response latency and pessimal on completion time, which would sharpen what a stated latency objective actually measures.

Use the quantum-versus-switch-cost arithmetic (10 ms slice against 1 ms switch, then a 100 ms slice for amortization) as a compact illustration of why pool sizing and yield frequency trade throughput for responsiveness.
Does the measurement page distinguish first-response latency from completion time over a finite observation window?

notes: Source claim: MLFQ originated with Corbato et al.'s 1962 CTSS work and is presented as a way to approximate short-job-first scheduling without knowing job length in advance.
Source claim: Rules 1-2 make priority strict across queues and round-robin within one, while Rules 3-4 move a job down as it consumes its per-level allotment.

notes: The chapter traces multiprocessor ubiquity to power constraints that slowed single-core gains, then states the scheduling problem rather than assuming parallelism is free (source claim, introduction).
Coherence is assigned to hardware via bus snooping; the text notes that write-back caches complicate invalidation but does not derive a protocol (source claim, §10.1).
A coherent shared memory still permits the Figure 10.3 list race, so the chapter treats locks as a correctness requirement and only then raises their performance cost (source claim, §10.2).
Cache affinity is explicitly a performance heuristic: correct execution on a different CPU is preserved, but warm cache and TLB state are lost (source claim, §10.3).
SQMS is characterized as easy to retrofit and load-balanced by construction, with a single lock as the scaling bottleneck and cross-CPU job motion as the affinity cost (source claim, §10.4).
The MQMS examples show imbalance appearing even with equal initial queue lengths: after C exits, A receives twice the CPU of B and D, and after A and C exit one CPU has no work (source claim, §10.5).
Work stealing is presented with an unresolved polling-frequency trade-off; the chapter offers no threshold, measurement, or proof of convergence (source claim, §10.5).

Linux's O(1)/CFS (multi-queue) and BFS (single-queue) are cited as coexisting designs, which supports the inference that queue topology alone does not determine scheduler suitability (source claim plus inference, §10.6).
The closing warning that small code changes produce large behavioral differences is a design caution, not an empirical finding; the chapter reports no measurements of its own (inference, §10.7).

The homework asks readers to predict and then verify warm-cache speedup, affinity pinning, and super-linear speedup with multi.py; no simulator results are included in the text (source claim, Homework).

tycho_candidates.candidate: Add a single global run-queue lock as a concrete contention mechanism: it bounds scheduling scalability even when total CPU capacity is sufficient, and lock alternatives have their own scaling limits.
Use a shared list pop as a compact worked example that cache coherence does not enforce compound invariants; a mutex restores correctness at the cost of serializing the critical section.

Contrast one central work queue with per-worker queues: per-worker ownership improves locality and removes a global lock, but static assignment creates idle capacity and unequal shares unless work migrates.
Treat repeated job migration as control-loop churn: require a minimum imbalance threshold and residency interval before moving work, otherwise balancing overhead can cancel the capacity it seeks.

notes: Source claim: Lu et al. classify 105 concurrency bugs from MySQL, Apache, Mozilla and OpenOffice into 74 non-deadlock and 31 deadlock bugs, with Mozilla contributing 41 non-deadlock and 16 deadlock cases and MySQL 14 and 9.

Source claim: 97% of the non-deadlock bugs in that study are either atomicity violations or order violations, which the authors use to argue that review and automated checking should concentrate on those two patterns.

Source claim: the MySQL atomicity example crashes because the non-NULL check and the fputs() use are not atomic against another thread setting proc_info to NULL; the fix locks the whole check-and-use region, not just the store.

Source claim: the Mozilla order violation assumes mThread is initialized before mMain() reads mThread->State; the fix adds a condition variable plus an mtInit state flag so the reader waits when it arrives first and proceeds when it arrives second.
Source claim: the four Coffman conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait) are jointly required, so each prevention technique is described as removing one of them.

Source claim: lock-address ordering lets a routine such as do_something(m1, m2) acquire two caller-supplied locks consistently regardless of argument order; inference: this presupposes a total order on addresses and a guarantee that m1 and m2 are distinct, which the code comment states as an assumption rather than checks.

Source claim: trylock-and-retry removes hold-and-wait but can livelock, mitigated by a random delay, and it must unwind any other resources acquired since the retry label, such as memory allocated after taking L1.

Source claim: the lock-free list insert spins on CompareAndSwap(&head, n->next, n) until it wins; inference: the listing omits reclamation of the node whose swap failed, so a real implementation must free or retire that node or it leaks under contention.

Source claim: scheduling-based avoidance needs advance knowledge of each thread's lock set and, in the second contention table, forces T1, T2 and T3 onto one processor, which removes deadlock by sacrificing parallelism; the authors call it viable mainly in embedded systems with full task knowledge.

Source claim: detect-and-recover runs a periodic resource-graph cycle check, which is standard in database systems but coarse for an operating system, where the pragmatic response to a rare freeze is a reboot (Tom West's Law).

tycho_candidates.candidate: Atomicity and order violations as the two dominant non-deadlock classes (97% of the studied bugs), giving a concrete checklist for reviewing check-then-act code around shared fields.

Hold-and-wait deadlock in request paths that keep a pooled connection while calling a slow dependency, with lock ordering and trylock backoff as the two practical remedies and livelock as the cost of the latter.
Deadlock detection as periodic resource-graph cycle checking versus reboot-and-recover pragmatism, as a framing for thread-dump-based diagnosis and its limits.
Total ordering by lock address as a mechanical way to make multi-lock acquisition safe without global knowledge of the call graph.

notes: Source claim: event-based concurrency is motivated by two problems, the difficulty of writing correct multi-threaded code and the programmer's weak control over what the OS schedules.

Source claim: the canonical event loop repeatedly fetches ready events and runs one handler at a time; because only one handler is active, the choice of which event to handle next is the scheduling decision.
Source claim: select() reports readability, writability and exceptional conditions across descriptor sets, rewrites those sets to the ready subset, and returns the number of ready descriptors.
Source claim: the timeout argument changes the waiting policy, with NULL blocking indefinitely and zero turning select() into an immediate poll; poll() offers a similar facility.

Source claim: the event-loop contract forbids blocking calls, because one handler waiting on a slow open() or read() stops every other connection, whereas a thread-based server lets other threads run during the wait.
Source claim: asynchronous I/O fills an aiocb with descriptor, offset, buffer and length, returns before completion, and is observed either by polling aio_error() or by a completion signal.
Source claim: when native asynchronous I/O is unavailable, a hybrid design can use events for network processing and a thread pool for outstanding I/O requests.
Source claim: state that a thread would keep on its stack must be packaged manually; a continuation keyed by the completing descriptor restores the socket descriptor needed to finish the event.

Source claim: multicore event servers must run handlers in parallel and therefore reintroduce locks, page faults are implicit blocking, and routines that change from non-blocking to blocking force handlers to be split.

Inference: select() readiness does not by itself prove a handler cannot block, so the no-blocking rule depends on non-blocking descriptors, bounded handler work and memory residency rather than on the polling API alone.

notes: Source claim: the interface is a flat array of 512-byte sectors numbered 0 to n-1; multi-sector operations are possible, but the only atomicity guarantee is a single 512-byte write, so a power loss can leave a torn write.
Source claim: the "unwritten contract" of disks (Schlosser and Ganger) is that nearby blocks and contiguous runs are faster, an assumption clients make but the interface does not promise.
Source claim: I/O time is seek plus rotational delay plus transfer, and the average rotational delay is half a rotation derived from RPM; 15,000 RPM implies 4 ms per rotation and 2 ms average delay.

Source claim: in the worked two-drive comparison, 4 KB random reads yield about 0.66 MB/s on the Cheetah and 0.31 MB/s on the Barracuda, while sequential 100 MB transfers approach 125 and 105 MB/s, a gap of roughly 200 to 300 times.

Source claim: SSTF orders by nearest track and can starve distant requests; SCAN sweeps back and forth, F-SCAN freezes the queue per sweep, C-SCAN sweeps one direction for fairness, and SPTF adds rotation but is usually implemented inside the drive.
Source claim: track skew offsets sector numbering across adjacent tracks so cross-track sequential reads avoid nearly a full rotational wait, and multi-zone drives put more sectors on outer tracks.

Source claim: drives carry an 8-16 MB cache, and write-back caching acknowledges before the data reaches the platter, which the chapter calls dangerous for ordering-sensitive file systems and defers to the journaling chapter.
Source claim: the familiar one-third average-seek figure comes from average seek distance under a uniform model, not from measured seek time.
Inference: the three-term equation is service time for one isolated request, so it is a lower bound on observed latency; queueing, request merging and OS batching sit outside it.

Inference: every policy described is greedy and only helps when the queue is deeper than one, so the chapter's practical advice reduces to batching requests and keeping sequential and random traffic apart.

notes: Source claim: a RAID presents a linear array of blocks and maps each logical request to one or more physical disks, and the chapter credits transparency (it can replace a SCSI disk with no host or OS change) for much of RAID's adoption.

Source claim: designs are compared on capacity, reliability and performance under a fail-stop fault model in which a disk is either fully working or permanently lost, failure is immediately detectable, and silent corruption or latent sector errors are deferred to the data-integrity chapter.

Source claim: RAID-0 striping yields N·B capacity, no fault tolerance, N·S sequential and N·R random bandwidth; chunk size trades intra-file parallelism (small chunks) against positioning time (large chunks), and no universally best size exists.

Source claim: RAID-1 mirroring halves useful capacity, certainly tolerates one failure (up to N/2 if the right disks fail), matches single-disk read latency, and reaches only (N/2)·S sequential bandwidth because each disk serves every other block and idles over the skipped one.
Source claim: RAID-4 keeps one XOR parity block per stripe, giving (N−1)·B capacity and one-failure tolerance; full-stripe writes are efficient, but any partial write must also update parity.

Source claim: RAID-4's dedicated parity disk serializes concurrent small writes, so random write throughput is R/2 and does not improve as data disks are added; RAID-5 rotates parity and reaches N/4·R because each small write still costs four physical I/Os.

Source claim: subtractive parity computes P_new = (C_old XOR C_new) XOR P_old with two reads and two writes, whereas additive parity reads every other data block in the stripe; the chapter asks the reader to find the crossover point.

Source claim: the consistent-update problem leaves mirrored copies divergent if a crash interrupts a multi-disk write, and the general fix is a write-ahead log, usually held in battery-backed non-volatile RAM because logging every write to disk is prohibitively expensive.

Inference: the throughput matrix is an analytical upper bound, not a measurement; it assumes independent disks, no controller or interconnect ceiling, and workloads that are purely sequential or purely random, and the chapter itself notes max-of-two-seeks effects make mirrored writes slightly worse than modeled.

Inference: parity RAID does not eliminate write cost, it relocates it into per-write amplification, so choosing RAID-5 over RAID-1 is really a claim about small-write concurrency and acceptable degraded-mode behavior rather than about capacity alone.

notes: Source claim: a file is a linear array of bytes with a low-level inode number, and a directory is a list of (user-readable name, low-level name) pairs that can nest into a tree rooted at /; the name's extension is convention only.

Source claim: open() with O_CREAT|O_WRONLY|O_TRUNC creates or truncates a file and returns a per-process descriptor, an opaque capability that indexes a per-process array of struct file pointers (xv6: ofile[NOFILE]).

Source claim: descriptors 0, 1 and 2 are standard input, output and error, so the first user open is normally 3; read() returns the bytes read and 0 at end of file, and each read or write implicitly advances the current offset.

Source claim: lseek() changes only an in-memory offset and performs no disk I/O, although reading at scattered offsets afterwards can cause seeks; the offset lives in the open file table entry, not in the inode.

Source claim: fork() makes parent and child share one open file table entry with an incremented reference count, so the child's lseek(10) is visible to the parent; dup() creates a second descriptor for the same entry and underlies shell redirection.

Source claim: write() is buffered and may return before data is persistent; fsync(fd) forces the file's dirty data, a newly created name also needs its containing directory fsynced, and because rename() is crash-atomic, write-temp/fsync/rename is the idiom for atomic file replacement.

Source claim: unlink() removes one name and decrements the inode link count, freeing data only at zero; hard links cannot cross partitions or target directories, whereas symbolic links are separate files holding a pathname and can dangle after the target is removed.

Source claim: permission bits encode owner/group/other read-write-execute, and on a directory the execute bit gates traversal; AFS access control lists provide per-directory, per-principal rights beyond that model.

Source claim: TOCTTOU attacks exploit the gap between a privileged check (for example lstat()) and the later use of the same path, as when a mailbox is renamed to /etc/passwd in between; O_NOFOLLOW, fewer privileged services and transactional file systems only narrow the problem.

Inference: the chapter specifies durability by API composition (fsync the file, fsync the directory, rename) but leaves the file system's internal ordering and metadata-journaling obligations to later chapters, so the guarantee is stated rather than derived here.

notes: Source claim: the old UNIX file system kept a superblock, inodes and data blocks and delivered only 2% of overall disk bandwidth in the McKusick et al. measurement, because it ignored positioning costs and fragmented free space, while 512-byte blocks worsened transfer efficiency.

Source claim: FFS introduced cylinder groups, later block groups because modern disks hide geometry, each holding a superblock copy, inode bitmap, data bitmap, inode table and data blocks so related data can be co-located and seeks shortened.

Source claim: FFS places a directory in a group with few allocated directories and many free inodes, puts a file's data in its inode's group, and puts all files of one directory in that directory's group.

Source claim: SEER traces show about 7% of opens repeat the previous file, nearly 40% are the same file or same directory, and another 25% are at tree distance two, as in proj/src/foo.c followed by proj/obj/foo.o, a pattern FFS does not capture.

Source claim: the large-file exception keeps the first 12 direct blocks with the inode and places each subsequent indirect chunk in a different group, so one large file does not fill the group and crowd out related files.

Source claim: spreading a large file hurts sequential throughput, so chunk size must amortize positioning; at 40MB/s and 10ms positioning, 409.6KB yields 50% of peak bandwidth, 3.6MB yields 90% and 39.6MB yields 99%.

Source claim: with 4KB blocks and 32-bit addresses, FFS placed every 1024 blocks (4MB) in a separate group, except the first 48KB reached by direct pointers, and the chapter argues rising transfer rates make mechanical costs relatively more expensive over time.
Source claim: FFS added 512-byte sub-blocks for small files, promoted them to a full 4KB block when the file grew, and mostly avoided the copy cost by having libc buffer writes into 4KB chunks.

Source claim: FFS staggered consecutive blocks by a parameterized skip to avoid a full rotation between sequential reads, accepting at most 50% of peak bandwidth; modern drives read a whole track into a buffer, making the trick unnecessary.
Inference: FFS placement optimizes namespace proximity rather than measured inter-open distance, so the roughly 25% distance-two share is a known locality class the policy leaves to seek time.

notes: Source claim: the crash-consistency problem is that any two on-disk writes can be separated by a crash, so a multi-block update may persist only partially.

Source claim: the append example enumerates six crash outcomes from three writes (inode, bitmap, data); two-write outcomes leave metadata self-consistent but the inode may point at garbage, while one-write outcomes yield inconsistency or a space leak.

Source claim: the log is treated as circular with a journal superblock tracking oldest/newest non-checkpointed transactions, and batching groups many updates into one global transaction to cut journal traffic.

Source claim: metadata (ordered) journaling omits user data from the log but must write data blocks before the commit block, since otherwise replay can leave an inode pointing at garbage; ext3 offers data, ordered and unordered modes.
Source claim: block reuse after delete can make replay overwrite live data, which ext3 addresses with revoke records that suppress replay of revoked blocks.

Source claim: alternatives are Soft Updates (careful write ordering, requiring per-structure knowledge), copy-on-write (ZFS), backpointer-based consistency, and optimistic crash consistency via generalized transaction checksums.

notes: Source claim: LFS rests on four motivations - growing memory caches shifting traffic to writes, a widening random-versus-sequential I/O gap, FFS paying many short seeks per file creation, and RAID-4/5 small-write penalties.
Source claim: updates are buffered in an in-memory segment and written sequentially to a free location; LFS never overwrites in place, so all writes can become large sequential transfers.

Source claim: buffering size is derived from positioning time and transfer rate, with D = F/(1-F) x Rpeak x Tposition; the worked example gives about 9 MB to reach 90% of peak on a 10 ms, 100 MB/s disk.

Source claim: because inodes are scattered and move on every update, an inode map translates inode number to latest on-disk address, and pieces of the imap are written adjacent to the data and inodes they describe.
Source claim: the checkpoint region is a fixed location pointing to the latest imap pieces, updated only periodically (about every 30 seconds), which bounds the seek cost of finding the map.
Source claim: the imap also solves the recursive update problem, since a moved inode changes only its imap entry, not the parent directory entry that stores the inode number.

Source claim: overwriting to new locations produces garbage; cleaning works segment-by-segment, reading M segments and compacting live blocks into N new segments (N < M), and liveness is decided via a segment summary block holding inode number and offset plus a check of the inode pointer.
Source claim: the original policy cleans cold segments sooner and hot segments later, waiting for hot blocks to die; later adaptive work improved on this heuristic.
Source claim: crash recovery uses two checkpoint regions written alternately with timestamped header and final block, and roll forward replays segments after the last consistent CR.

Inference: LFS trades a write-path cost (cleaning, roughly a garbage-collection tax on free space) for sequential write efficiency, so its viability depends on cleaner efficiency keeping segment utilization high enough; the chapter states the trade-off but gives no utilization bound or cleaning-cost model.

notes: Source claim: the fail-stop model is incomplete; a disk can return an error for one block (LSE) or plausible but wrong data (silent corruption), so whole-disk health is not a data-integrity guarantee (45.1).

Source claim: a three-year study of roughly 1.5 million drives reported at least one LSE on 9.40% of cheap and 1.40% of costly drives, and corruption on 0.50% and 0.05%; these are fleet observations, not per-read probabilities (45.1).

Source claim: LSEs are detectable, so mirroring or parity can reconstruct the block; during RAID-4/5 rebuild, a second LSE can defeat reconstruction, motivating dual-parity schemes such as RAID-DP (45.2).
Source claim: a checksum stores a small digest with data; equality makes corruption unlikely but not impossible, and a mismatch identifies corruption without supplying a good copy (45.3-45.4).

Source claim: XOR checksums miss paired bit flips in the same position; additive checksums are weak under byte shifts; Fletcher detects all single- and double-bit errors and many bursts; CRC uses a polynomial remainder; collisions remain possible for every scheme (45.3).

Source claim: checksum placement changes I/O cost: an 8-byte checksum fits a 520-byte sector with one write, whereas grouping checksums in 512-byte sectors can require a read-modify-write of the checksum sector (45.3).

Source claim: adding disk and block identifiers detects misdirected writes because the stored location metadata will not match the read location; it does not detect a lost write, whose old contents and old metadata still agree (45.5-45.6).

Source claim: lost writes need read-after-write verification or a checksum held at a different level, such as ZFS's inode or indirect-block checksum; losing both data and metadata updates can still evade detection (45.6).

Source claim: scrubbing periodically reads all blocks to validate checksums; an 8-byte checksum per 4-KB block is about 0.19% capacity overhead, while CPU, extra I/O and scrub scheduling are the time costs (45.7-45.8).

Inference: checksum algorithm, placement, coverage and recovery source are independent choices; a strong checksum over the wrong scope can still miss a lost or misdirected update, and detection without redundancy only converts silent corruption into an error.

tycho_candidates.candidate: Require an explicit byte-integrity contract for uploads: checksum algorithm, scope, trusted expected value and verification point; a stored checksum cannot repair corruption without an independent good copy.
Add a data-verification step to restore drills: read back restored data, compare checksums and test detection of silent corruption, not only row counts or command success.

Distinguish integrity evidence from retention and access control: checksums can detect alteration but do not prove authorship or authority, and a valid stored checksum may accompany stale or lost data.

notes: Source claim: the chapter makes failure, not performance, the defining problem of distributed systems, then reframes it as an opportunity because a collection of regularly failing machines can present a service that rarely fails. Inference: this is an availability argument about aggregation, not a correctness guarantee, and it leaves correlated failure domains unaddressed.

Source claim: packet loss is treated as unavoidable even if every link and host works, because router and endpoint buffers are finite and overflow forces drops. Inference: loss and overload are the same phenomenon observed at different scales, which is why the chapter's timeout advice later turns into a load argument.

Source claim: UDP is presented as a deliberately unreliable datagram layer whose checksum guards against corruption but not loss, with the end-to-end argument used to justify leaving reliability to applications. Inference: a checksum is a corruption detector, not an integrity proof, and the text gives no residual error rate.

Source claim: reliable messaging is assembled from acknowledgments plus timeout/retry, and duplicates appear when the acknowledgment rather than the request is lost. Inference: the same event produces different sender and receiver histories, which is the ambiguity that later shows up as retry-induced duplicate effects.

Source claim: a per-sender sequence counter compared against a single expected value suppresses duplicates with bounded memory, unlike remembering every message ID. Inference: the scheme silently assumes one outstanding message per sender in order; pipelining or reordering would need a window or a larger counter space, which the chapter does not develop.

Source claim: RPC aims to make remote execution look like a local call, with a stub generator automating marshaling and a run-time library handling naming, transport, fragmentation, and long-running calls. Inference: the 'looks local' promise is exactly where latency, partial failure, and serialization semantics leak into the programming model.

Source claim: reliable transport such as TCP adds two extra acknowledgment messages per request/response, so many RPC packages run over UDP and reimplement reliability, yielding exactly-once only without failure and at-most-once when failure occurs. Inference: duplicate suppression therefore becomes a server-side obligation, and 'exactly once' is scoped far more narrowly than the phrase suggests.

Source claim: the timeout value trades wasted retransmission and CPU against slow loss detection, and exponential back-off from the Aloha/Ethernet lineage avoids retry storms when loss signals server overload. Inference: a fixed timeout encodes an assumption about the latency distribution, so adaptive timeouts act as overload control as much as performance tuning.

Source claim: DSM failed in practice because a failed machine makes parts of the shared address space disappear, breaking pointer-based structures, while remote page faults make access cost unpredictable. Inference: the chapter uses this as a caution about extending local-memory abstractions across a failure boundary, not as a proof that no shared-memory design can work.

Source claim: the end-to-end argument holds that only the application can verify end-to-end reliability, since bytes can be corrupted in sender memory or on receiver disk after a reliable transfer, yet lower-layer machinery may still be justified for performance. Inference: this is a principle about where final verification must live, not a blanket prohibition on retries at more than one layer.

Long-running RPC handling via explicit acknowledgment plus periodic status polling; useful as a precedent for progress signals distinct from completion, relevant to deadline budgets.
